pitfall: Ammonia can be markedly elevated with entirely normal transaminases — do not require liver injury before making the diagnosis. Lactulose does nothing here; the mechanism is carnitine depletion and urea cycle inhibition.

dose:
1 g pyridoxine per gram of isoniazid ingested
Unknown quantity: 70 mg/kg IV, up to 5 g
Give over 5–10 min; repeat if seizures persist
pitfall: Benzodiazepines alone will not stop these seizures — the defect is GABA synthesis, and only pyridoxine restores it. Most emergency departments stock a few hundred milligrams, nowhere near the five grams a real ingestion requires. Confirm your actual stock now, not during the resuscitation.

dose: 25 mg/kg IV, may repeat to a maximum of 15–20 g/day
pitfall: Same mechanism as isoniazid, same stocking problem. Monomethylhydrazine also causes hepatotoxicity and hemolysis, so the seizures are not the whole illness.

dose:
Propranolol 1–3 mg IV or 20–40 mg PO for adrenergic symptoms
Cholestyramine 4 g PO QID to interrupt enterohepatic recirculation
Propylthiouracil and corticosteroids only in true thyroid storm
pitfall: Symptoms are delayed 2 to 7 days as T4 converts to T3 — a well child at 6 hours means nothing. Most pediatric levothyroxine exposures need only observation.

dose:
15 mg/kg/h IV infusion — faster rates cause hypotension
Label ceiling 6 g/24 h; toxicology practice commonly exceeds it in severe poisoning
Indications: serum iron >500 µg/dL, shock, acidosis, persistent vomiting, or radiopaque tablets on film
Stop when acidosis resolves and urine colour normalizes, typically <24 h
pitfall: Activated charcoal does not bind iron — whole bowel irrigation is the decontamination method. Vin rosé urine is neither sensitive nor specific and should not be your endpoint. Infusions beyond 24 hours are linked to ARDS and to Yersinia enterocolitica sepsis. Iron levels drawn late are falsely reassuring as iron distributes into tissue.

dose:
BAL 4 mg/kg deep IM q4h — start FIRST
CaNa₂EDTA 1500 mg/m²/day continuous infusion, beginning 4 h after BAL
Continue 5 days, then reassess
pitfall: Order matters: EDTA alone in encephalopathy redistributes lead into the brain and can kill. Never substitute disodium EDTA for calcium disodium EDTA — that error causes fatal hypocalcemia and has done so repeatedly. BAL is suspended in peanut oil, so document the allergy history.

dose:
10 mg/kg PO q8h × 5 days, then 10 mg/kg q12h × 14 days
The only FDA-approved oral lead chelator; edetate calcium disodium and dimercaprol are the approved parenteral ones
Labelled for children 1 year and older with blood lead above 45 µg/dL; at least 2 weeks between courses
pitfall: Chelation without removing the exposure source is pointless and rebound is guaranteed — environmental abatement is part of the prescription. Chelation below 45 µg/dL has not improved neurodevelopmental outcomes and is not recommended. Succimer is the only oral option, not the only approved one — penicillamine is the agent with no lead indication at all. Forty-five is a guideline figure rather than a hard cut, and CDC's reference value of 3.5 µg/dL identifies exposure for follow-up; it is not a chelation threshold.

sources.label: AAP, Treatment of Lead Poisoning, updated April 2025

agentLine: Dimercaprol, transitioning to succimer or DMPS
dose:
BAL 3–5 mg/kg IM q4h initially, then oral succimer 10 mg/kg q8h
Aggressive fluid resuscitation; monitor QT
pitfall: Arsine gas is a completely different disease — massive hemolysis and renal failure — and chelation does not work; it needs exchange transfusion and dialysis. Do not treat the two the same way.

dose:
Inorganic salts: DMPS is preferred where available; succimer 10 mg/kg q8h otherwise
Elemental vapor: supportive, chelation of limited value
pitfall: Dimercaprol is contraindicated in methylmercury poisoning — it redistributes mercury into the central nervous system and worsens neurologic injury. This is the opposite of its role in inorganic mercury.

dose:
Penicillamine 250–500 mg PO QID; trientine 750–1500 mg/day
Zinc acetate 50 mg TID for maintenance
pitfall: Penicillamine causes paradoxical neurologic worsening in a substantial minority of neurologic Wilson disease at initiation — trientine is the safer start. Acute copper sulfate ingestion causes hemolysis and hepatic necrosis and behaves like a different illness.

dose:
Adults and adolescents 3 g PO three times daily; children 2–12 y, 1 g three times daily
Continue until urinary thallium falls; treatment often runs 30 days or more
Multi-dose activated charcoal is a reasonable adjunct
pitfall: Alopecia and painful ascending neuropathy appear late; by the time the hair falls out, the exposure is one to two weeks old. Hemodialysis is only useful very early.

dose:
Adults 3 g PO TID; children 2–12 y, 1 g TID
Continue for 30 days or longer, guided by bioassay
pitfall: Prussian blue does nothing for plutonium, americium, uranium, or iodine — matching the agent to the isotope is the whole exercise. Aquarium-grade or artist's pigment Prussian blue is not the pharmaceutical product.

dose:
Ca-DTPA 1 g IV over 3–4 min or nebulized, within the first 24 h
Switch to Zn-DTPA 1 g daily for maintenance
Both NDAs are discontinued and the NDC is inactivated — obtain through Golden State Medical Supply, 1-805-477-9866, or REAC/TS
pitfall: Ca-DTPA is more effective early but depletes essential trace metals with repeated use — the switch to Zn-DTPA at 24 hours is not optional. Avoid DTPA in uranium and neptunium contamination because of nephrotoxicity.

dose:
Adults and adolescents ≥70 kg: 130 mg PO once daily
Children 3–18 y: 65 mg · 1 month–3 y: 32 mg · neonates <1 month: 16 mg
Repeat daily only while exposure risk persists
Greatest benefit immediately before or within a few hours of exposure; efficacy falls steeply thereafter
pitfall: KI blocks thyroid uptake of radioiodine and nothing else — it is useless for cesium, strontium, or any other isotope, and taking it 'for radiation' is a common public misconception. Contraindicated in iodine allergy and dermatitis herpetiformis.
window: Greatest benefit before or within a few hours of exposure

sources.label: FDA KI guidance for radiation emergencies

dose:
Filgrastim 10 µg/kg/day SC; pegfilgrastim 6 mg SC weekly × 2
Sargramostim 7 µg/kg/day; romiplostim 10 µg/kg SC × 1 (approved January 2021)
Start as soon as exposure to a myelosuppressive dose is suspected
pitfall: All were approved under the Animal Rule — dose from the label, not from oncology practice. Lymphocyte depletion kinetics in the first 48 hours are your best early dosimeter when physical dosimetry is unavailable.

sources.label: FDA MCM approvals under the Animal Rule

dose:
Supportive; extremely high mortality
Protect staff — phosphine gas is released from gastric contents
pitfall: Gastric lavage effluent and vomitus liberate phosphine. Health-care workers have been poisoned by treating these patients in enclosed spaces without ventilation.

dose:
CroFab: 4–6 vials to initial control, repeat until control, then 2 vials at 6, 12, and 18 h
Anavip: 10 vials to initial control, then 4 vials as needed; maintenance rarely required
Both FDA-approved for all North American pit viper envenomation
pitfall: CroFab's shorter half-life produces recurrent thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy days later, which is why the maintenance schedule exists and why patients need follow-up labs after discharge. Anavip's longer-lived F(ab')₂ largely avoids this. No tourniquets, no incision, no suction, no ice, no electricity — all of these add injury without removing venom.

sources.label: Unified Treatment Algorithm, BMC Emerg Med 2011

dose:
3–5 vials IV for a credible bite, repeat as needed
Supply is limited; contact poison control early to locate stock
pitfall: Neurotoxicity is delayed up to 12 hours and then progresses to respiratory failure. Treat on the basis of a credible bite; waiting for symptoms means intubating before the antivenom arrives. Local findings are minimal and falsely reassuring.
window: Before neurotoxicity, which is delayed up to 12 h

sources.label: North American Coral Snake Antivenin prescribing information

dose:
Initial dose 3 vials, diluted to 50 mL, IV over 10 min
Then 1 vial at a time at 30–60 min intervals for persistent symptoms
Monitor closely during and for 60 min after the infusion
pitfall: Grade III–IV envenomation in small children — opsoclonus, roving eye movements, thrashing — is often mistaken for a seizure or dystonic reaction. Benzodiazepine sedation alone risks respiratory failure and a prolonged ICU stay that antivenom prevents.

dose:
1 vial diluted in 50 mL saline over 30 min; repeat once if needed
Opioids and benzodiazepines for pain and spasm
pitfall: This is whole IgG, not a Fab fragment, so anaphylaxis and serum sickness rates are appreciably higher than with modern antivenoms. Reserve it for severe envenomation — refractory pain, hypertensive crisis, pregnancy with abdominal rigidity — rather than routine bites.

agentLine: No antivenom available in the US
dose:
Wound care, tetanus prophylaxis, observation
Monitor for systemic loxoscelism: hemolysis, DIC, renal failure — mostly in children
pitfall: Dapsone, steroids, and early excision are all popular and none are supported. Most necrotic wounds attributed to recluse spiders in areas outside their range are something else, usually MRSA.

agentLine: Hot water immersion; stonefish antivenom where stocked
dose:
Immerse in water at 42–45°C for 30–90 min — heat denatures the venom
Radiograph for retained barb; these are heavily contaminated wounds
pitfall: Test the water on the caregiver's own skin: analgesia from the venom means the patient cannot report a scald until it has happened. Retained spine fragments cause the delayed infections and are easily missed.

sources.label: Wilderness Medical Society practice guidelines, marine envenomation

agentLine: BAT heptavalent botulism antitoxin (equine, types A–G)
dose:
One vial IV, weight-adjusted in children
Obtained through the state health department and the CDC Emergency Operations Center: 770-488-7100
pitfall: Antitoxin binds only circulating toxin — it halts progression but reverses nothing already bound at the nerve terminal. Every hour of diagnostic hesitation is permanent paralysis. Give it on clinical suspicion; do not wait for laboratory confirmation, which takes days. Descending, symmetric, bulbar-first weakness with a clear sensorium is the pattern.

dose:
50 mg/kg (1 mL/kg) IV as a single infusion, through a dedicated line
Start at 0.5 mL/kg/h; if tolerated at 15 min, increase to 1 mL/kg/h — do not exceed
Available only from the California Infant Botulism Treatment and Prevention Program: 510-231-7600
pitfall: Do not give equine BAT to an infant if BabyBIG is obtainable — the human product avoids serum sickness and shortens hospital stay by weeks. Aminoglycosides potentiate the neuromuscular blockade and should be avoided for any concurrent infection.

agentLine: Human tetanus immune globulin + metronidazole + wound debridement
dose:
HTIG 3000–6000 units IM, part infiltrated around the wound
Metronidazole 500 mg IV q6–8h (preferred over penicillin)
Benzodiazepines, magnesium infusion, and often neuromuscular blockade for spasms
pitfall: Penicillin is a GABA antagonist and may worsen spasms; metronidazole is the better choice. Immune globulin does not touch toxin already fixed to neurons, so the illness still runs its weeks-long course. Active immunization is still required — the disease does not confer immunity.

dose:
20,000–120,000 units by clinical severity and duration
Available through CDC under IND; call the Emergency Operations Center
pitfall: Sensitivity testing before administration is required — this is horse serum with a meaningful anaphylaxis rate. Antibiotics stop transmission but do not neutralize toxin; only antitoxin does, and only before it binds.

agentLine: Raxibacumab, obiltoxaximab, or anthrax immune globulin IV
dose:
Raxibacumab 40 mg/kg IV; obiltoxaximab 16 mg/kg IV — both with premedication for infusion reactions
Always combined with two-drug antimicrobial therapy plus a protein synthesis inhibitor
pitfall: Monoclonals target protective antigen and are adjuncts, never monotherapy. Pleural effusions must be drained — they are toxin reservoirs, and drainage independently improves survival.

agentLine: No FDA-approved therapy; IV silibinin (investigational), NAC, penicillin G
dose:
Aggressive IV crystalloid to maintain renal elimination
Silibinin (Legalon SIL) 5 mg/kg load then 20 mg/kg/day continuous — the US expanded-access protocol terminated in 2020 and no active supply pathway remains; single-patient IND is the only route
NAC and high-dose penicillin G, both off-label; activated charcoal, multi-dose
Early transplant centre referral
pitfall: The 6- to 24-hour symptom-free latency is the trap: a patient with a normal panel at presentation may already be committed to hepatic failure. Any gastrointestinal illness beginning six or more hours after a foraged mushroom meal is amatoxin until proven otherwise. Silibinin's US pivotal trial was terminated without analysis, so the evidence base remains observational.
window: Before the hepatic phase; latency is 6–24 h

sources.label: MMWR, Amanita ocreata poisoning cluster, May 2026

dose: Supportive; decontamination; aggressive fluid resuscitation for the GI form
pitfall: Inhalational exposure produces delayed pulmonary edema at 8 to 24 hours. There is no antidote and no useful chelation — resist the pressure to give something.

dose:
Benzodiazepines first and generously
Cyproheptadine 12 mg PO, then 2 mg q2h until response (max 32 mg/day)
Hyperthermia >41.1°C: intubate, paralyze with a non-depolarizing agent, cool aggressively
pitfall: Hyperthermia from sustained muscle activity is what kills, and it is the one thing that must be treated within minutes. Paralysis stops heat production; antipyretics do nothing because the hypothalamic set point is normal. Physical restraints worsen isometric contraction and lactate. Avoid succinylcholine if rhabdomyolysis has raised potassium.

sources.label: Boyer & Shannon, serotonin syndrome, N Engl J Med 2005

agentLine: Stop the antipsychotic; dantrolene, bromocriptine, benzodiazepines
dose:
Dantrolene 1–2.5 mg/kg IV, repeat to 10 mg/kg/day
Bromocriptine 2.5 mg PO q8h; amantadine 100 mg q8h as an alternative
Restart any abruptly withdrawn dopaminergic agent
pitfall: Onset is over days with lead-pipe rigidity and hyporeflexia — the opposite of serotonin syndrome's rapid onset, clonus, and hyperreflexia. Getting the two confused sends you to the wrong antidote. Withdrawal of levodopa or an abrupt dopamine agonist change causes an identical picture.

dose:
2.5 mg/kg IV rapidly, repeat q5–10 min to 10 mg/kg or more
Ryanodex 250 mg per vial reconstitutes in seconds; classic dantrolene needs 60 mL sterile water per 20 mg vial
Stop the trigger, hyperventilate with 100% oxygen, cool, treat hyperkalemia
MHAUS hotline 1-800-644-9737
pitfall: Reconstituting classic dantrolene is slow and requires several people — know which formulation your cart holds before the crisis. Non-triggering anesthesia does not exclude the diagnosis in a delayed presentation. Recrudescence occurs in up to a quarter of cases; continue dantrolene for 24 to 48 hours.

dose:
Diphenhydramine 25–50 mg IV/IM (pediatric 1 mg/kg)
Benztropine 1–2 mg IV/IM
Continue oral therapy for 48–72 h to prevent recurrence
pitfall: Failing to prescribe the 2- to 3-day oral course sends the patient back with the same reaction once the parenteral dose wears off. Oculogyric crisis and laryngeal dystonia are frequently misdiagnosed as seizure or anaphylaxis.

sources.label: Benztropine mesylate prescribing information — drug-induced extrapyramidal disorders

dose:
EXTRIP: dialyze if level >5.0 mEq/L, or >4.0 mEq/L with renal impairment, or with decreased consciousness, seizures, or dysrhythmias
Normal saline for volume repletion
pitfall: Activated charcoal does not bind lithium — sodium polystyrene is a theoretical alternative, whole bowel irrigation for sustained-release preparations. Levels rebound 6 to 8 hours after dialysis as lithium redistributes out of cells; recheck before deciding you are finished. Chronic toxicity is far more dangerous at any given level than acute.

dose:
Benzodiazepines, dark quiet environment, early paralysis and intubation
Monitor for rhabdomyolysis and hyperthermia
pitfall: Consciousness is preserved throughout — the patient feels everything. Sedate deeply. Any stimulus, including examination, provokes convulsions.

dose:
Over 70 kg: 100 mL bolus over 2–3 min, then ~250 mL over 15–20 min
Under 70 kg: 1.5 mL/kg bolus, then 0.25 mL/kg/min
Persistent instability: repeat the bolus and double the infusion rate
Continue the infusion at least 15 min after hemodynamic stability; maximum 12 mL/kg
ASRA 2020 checklist
pitfall: Reduce epinephrine to boluses of 1 µg/kg or less — standard ACLS doses impair resuscitation in LAST. Avoid vasopressin, calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers, and any further local anesthetic. Call for the lipid before you are sure you need it, and keep monitoring at least 4 to 6 hours after apparent recovery: relapse is documented. No lipid emulsion carries a labelled indication for this — every product is approved for parenteral nutrition, so the use is off-label and guideline-endorsed rather than an approved antidote. Twelve mL/kg is a hard ceiling, not an approximation.

sources.label: ASRA Checklist for Treatment of Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity, 2020 v1.1
Intralipid 20% prescribing information, rev. 5/2023 — parenteral nutrition indication only

dose:
2 mg/kg at reappearance of the second twitch
4 mg/kg at post-tetanic count 1–2
16 mg/kg for immediate reversal ~3 min after a single 1.2 mg/kg rocuronium dose
pitfall: It binds hormonal contraceptives — patients need seven days of backup contraception, and telling them is not optional. Marked bradycardia and asystole have been reported within minutes. It does nothing for succinylcholine or for benzylisoquinolinium agents such as cisatracurium and atracurium.

dose:
Neostigmine 0.03–0.07 mg/kg with glycopyrrolate 0.2 mg per 1 mg neostigmine
Requires at least some twitch response — will not reverse deep block
pitfall: Given at deep block it produces paradoxical weakness. Always confirm train-of-four before reversing, and never use it as a substitute for sugammadex in a can't-intubate-can't-oxygenate rescue.

sources.label: ASA practice guidelines for monitoring and antagonism of neuromuscular blockade, Anesthesiology 2023

dose:
Sedate and ventilate until spontaneous recovery, typically 4–8 h
Send a dibucaine number and counsel the family — it is heritable
pitfall: The error is assuming the patient is not waking for a neurologic reason. They are fully aware and paralyzed. Sedation is mandatory.

dose:
Topical 2.5% calcium gluconate gel, massaged in continuously
Intradermal 5% calcium gluconate 0.5 mL/cm² for refractory pain
Intra-arterial 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate in 40 mL D5W over 4 h for digits
IV calcium and magnesium for systemic toxicity; continuous ECG
pitfall: Concentrations below 20% cause delayed pain over hours with normal-looking skin, so the burn is routinely underestimated at triage. What kills is not the wound but profound hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, and hyperkalemia causing dysrhythmia — an exposure of 2% body surface area with concentrated HF can be fatal. Never inject calcium chloride into tissue; it causes necrosis.

dose:
2.5% calcium gluconate (2 mL of 10% in 3 mL saline) nebulized
Aggressive systemic calcium and magnesium replacement
pitfall: Airway edema can be delayed. Anyone with inhalational HF exposure needs admission and serial ionized calcium regardless of how they look at hour one.

dose:
WITHHOLD supplemental oxygen unless SpO₂ <90%
Fuller's earth or activated charcoal immediately if presenting early
Immunosuppression with cyclophosphamide and steroids is unproven
pitfall: Giving oxygen reflexively accelerates the redox cycling that destroys the lung — this is the one poisoning where routine oxygen is contraindicated. Even small ingestions of concentrate are lethal over days to weeks by progressive pulmonary fibrosis, and there is no rescue after the first hours.

dose:
No neutralization, no charcoal, no induced emesis, no blind NG placement
Early endoscopy at 12–24 h to grade injury; CT is increasingly used
Airway assessment first
pitfall: Attempting to neutralize generates an exothermic reaction and deepens the injury. Absence of oral burns does not exclude significant esophageal injury, particularly with alkalis and with liquid preparations.

dose:
No gastric emptying, no charcoal — aspiration is the injury
Supportive respiratory care; observe 6 h for chemical pneumonitis
pitfall: Avoid catecholamines where possible: halogenated and aromatic hydrocarbons sensitize the myocardium and epinephrine can precipitate ventricular fibrillation, which is the mechanism of sudden sniffing death.

dose:
Multi-dose activated charcoal 25 g q2–4h
HD for acute level >100 µg/mL, chronic >60 µg/mL, or seizures/dysrhythmia at any level
Esmolol 25–50 µg/kg/min for supraventricular tachycardia with hypotension
Replete potassium
pitfall: Hypokalemia here is intracellular shift, not deficit, and over-replacement causes rebound hyperkalemia once the drug clears. Chronic toxicity is dangerous at much lower levels than acute — the same number means different things.

dose:
Aggressive supportive care, G-CSF for marrow suppression
Anti-colchicine Fab exists only as historical French compassionate use
pitfall: The multiphasic course misleads: a GI phase, an apparent recovery, then multiorgan failure at 24 to 72 hours. Ingestions above 0.5 mg/kg have very high mortality. Do not discharge on the basis of improvement at 12 hours.

dose:
Dialyze for lactate >20 mmol/L, pH ≤7.0, shock, or failure to improve
Extended or repeated sessions are often required
pitfall: Bicarbonate infusion alone does not address the ongoing lactate production and can worsen intracellular acidosis. The decision to dialyze rests on the acidosis and the clinical trajectory, not on the metformin level, which is rarely available in time.

dose:
1 g/kg, maximum 50 g PO or by NG
Greatest benefit within 1 h; longer for anticholinergics, opioids, and sustained-release products
pitfall: Does not bind metals (iron, lithium, lead), alcohols, hydrocarbons, caustics, or potassium. Requires an intact or protected airway — aspiration of charcoal causes a severe, sometimes fatal pneumonitis, and is the reason routine use has fallen away.
window: Greatest benefit within 1 h of ingestion

sources.label: AACT/EAPCCT position paper: single-dose activated charcoal

dose:
25 g q2–4h after the initial dose
Established benefit: carbamazepine, dapsone, phenobarbital, quinine, theophylline
pitfall: Omit the sorbitol after the first dose — repeated cathartics cause dangerous fluid and electrolyte shifts, especially in children. Confirm bowel sounds before each dose; ileus turns this into an obstruction.

sources.label: AACT/EAPCCT position statement: multi-dose activated charcoal

dose:
1–2 L/h in adults, 500 mL/h in children, until the rectal effluent runs clear
Use for sustained-release calcium channel blockers and beta-blockers, iron, lead, and body packers
pitfall: Contraindicated with ileus, obstruction, perforation, hemodynamic instability, or an unprotected airway. It is labour-intensive and frequently abandoned halfway, which achieves nothing.

sources.label: AACT/EAPCCT position paper: whole bowel irrigation

dose:
150 mEq NaHCO₃ in 1 L D5W at 1.5–2× maintenance; target urine pH 7.5–8.0
Useful for salicylate, phenobarbital, methotrexate, chlorpropamide, 2,4-D
pitfall: Hypokalemia defeats alkalinization — the kidney exchanges potassium for hydrogen and acidifies the urine regardless of what you infuse. Replace potassium first and continuously.

dose:
EXTRIP has published recommendations for 13 poisonings: acetaminophen, barbiturates,
carbamazepine, digoxin, lithium, metformin, methanol, phenytoin, salicylates, thallium,
theophylline, tricyclic antidepressants, and valproate
Ethylene glycol and diethylene glycol are dialysed on separate, well-established grounds
High-flux, high blood-flow intermittent HD is preferred over CRRT for most
pitfall: CRRT clears far less per hour and is a poor substitute when the patient is dying of the toxin rather than of hemodynamic instability. Rebound after dialysis is expected with lithium, valproate, and methanol — recheck levels. Note that several EXTRIP recommendations are recommendations against dialysis, so citing the workgroup is not the same as citing support.

dose:
Consider early for a reversible cardiotoxin with refractory shock or arrest
Best-supported in calcium channel blocker, beta-blocker, and sodium channel blocker toxicity
pitfall: The determinant of survival is how early the conversation happens. A patient on four vasopressors is already late. Toxicologic arrest has better neurologic outcomes than most other ECPR indications, which should lower the threshold rather than raise it.

sources.label: AHA 2023 focused update: cardiac arrest in toxicity

dose:
Empiric 10–20 vials; response is less predictable than with digoxin
Serum digoxin assay cross-reacts but does not quantify the plant glycoside
Multi-dose activated charcoal; treat hyperkalaemia
pitfall: The digoxin level tells you exposure occurred, not how much Fab to give — dose to clinical and electrocardiographic response, not to a number. Yellow oleander seed ingestion is a common suicidal method outside the US and carries high mortality; a single seed can kill a child. Oleander grows throughout South Texas as an ornamental.

sources.label: MMWR and case series on Nerium and Thevetia cardiotoxicity

agentLine: None — benzodiazepines and barbiturates for seizures
dose:
Aggressive benzodiazepines, then barbiturate or propofol; early intubation and paralysis
Monitor for rhabdomyolysis, renal failure, and severe acidosis
pitfall: The most violently toxic plant in North America. Cicutoxin causes status epilepticus within 15–90 minutes, often refractory to standard doses. Frequently misidentified as wild parsnip, wild carrot, or water parsnip by foragers — the root is the most toxic part.
window: Seizures within 15–90 min of ingestion

dose:
Airway protection and mechanical ventilation until the alkaloid clears
Activated charcoal if early; monitor for rhabdomyolysis
pitfall: Ascending paralysis with a preserved sensorium — the patient is aware throughout. Death is respiratory, and survival is entirely a function of whether someone ventilates them. Distinguish from water hemlock, which seizes rather than paralyses; the two are commonly confused by name.

dose:
Sodium bicarbonate for QRS widening; magnesium and pacing for dysrhythmia
Digoxin Fab is ineffective — taxines are not cardiac glycosides
ECMO has been used successfully in massive ingestion
pitfall: Cardiac sodium and calcium channel blockade with wide-complex bradycardia progressing to asystole, typically within hours. There is no antidote, and reaching for digoxin Fab because the plant is a cardiotoxin wastes both time and vials. Ingestion of chewed needles is the lethal exposure; whole swallowed berries are usually benign because the seed passes intact.

dose:
Amiodarone or lidocaine for ventricular dysrhythmia; magnesium
Atropine for bradycardia; ECMO for refractory arrest
Activated charcoal early
pitfall: Perioral and limb paraesthesia followed by refractory ventricular dysrhythmia. Most Western cases follow herbal preparations, particularly imported traditional Chinese medicines where processing was inadequate. Standard antiarrhythmics often fail and ECMO is the intervention with the best reported outcomes.

agentLine: Physostigmine where obtainable; otherwise rivastigmine and supportive care
dose:
See the antimuscarinic delirium entries for agent detail
Benzodiazepines for agitation; active cooling; bladder scan for retention
pitfall: Deliberate ingestion by adolescents seeking hallucinations is the usual story, and the delirium lasts 24 to 48 hours — far longer than they expect. Seeds are the most concentrated part. Do not use antipsychotics: their antimuscarinic activity compounds the toxidrome and their alpha-blockade worsens hyperthermia.

dose:
Atropine 0.5–1 mg IV for symptomatic bradycardia, repeat as needed
IV fluids for hypotension; most resolve within 24 h
pitfall: Bradycardia and hypotension with a clear sensorium after eating flowers, leaves, or unprocessed honey. Almost all recover fully with atropine and fluids, so aggressive intervention is rarely warranted. Texas mountain laurel is a different plant — it contains cytisine and produces a nicotinic picture instead.

dose:
Benzodiazepines for agitation and myoclonus; supportive care
Atropine is contraindicated — this is not a muscarinic syndrome despite the name
pitfall: The name misleads: A. muscaria contains almost no muscarine. Giving atropine for a presumed cholinergic picture worsens the delirium. Expect an alternating pattern of agitation and somnolence over 6 to 24 hours with full recovery. This is not the deadly Amanita — that is A. phalloides or A. ocreata, which look nothing like it and behave nothing like it.

dose:
Supportive care; haemodialysis for established renal failure; transplant referral
No chelation or specific therapy exists
pitfall: Renal failure appears 2 to 20 days after ingestion, long after any gastrointestinal upset has resolved and the patient has stopped connecting the two. A normal creatinine at presentation means nothing. Anyone with a foraged mushroom meal and later unexplained renal failure should be asked about Cortinarius specifically.
window: Renal injury declares itself 2–20 days after ingestion

dose:
Fluid and electrolyte resuscitation; antiemetics
Observe for the late-onset pattern that would suggest amatoxin instead
pitfall: Symptom onset within 2 hours is reassuring and points here. Onset beyond 6 hours points to amatoxin, Gyromitra, or Cortinarius and changes the entire disposition. Timing of the first symptom is the single most useful piece of history in mushroom poisoning.

dose:
Airway assessment first; early intubation for stridor or drooling
Observe at least 4–6 h; endoscopy for persistent symptoms
No neutralisation, no charcoal, no induced emesis
pitfall: These behave far worse than ordinary detergent. Children develop rapid CNS depression, vomiting, and airway oedema, and deaths have occurred from aspiration and laryngeal swelling. Ocular exposure from a burst pod causes corneal injury and needs irrigation and slit-lamp examination.
window: Airway oedema can progress over the first hours

sources.label: AAP and CDC reports on detergent pod exposures

dose:
Benzodiazepines; airway protection
No charcoal if seizure risk is imminent — aspiration risk
Observe 4–6 h; symptoms begin within 5–90 min
pitfall: One of the classic one-pill-can-kill exposures: a few millilitres of concentrated camphor can seize a toddler within minutes. Onset is fast, so a child who is well at 4 hours is unlikely to deteriorate — but the early window is genuinely dangerous. Camphor is not a mothball ingredient in most current products; confirm which compound is involved.
window: Seizures within 5–90 min of ingestion

dose:
Manage exactly as salicylate poisoning — see that entry for alkalinisation and dialysis criteria
One teaspoon of oil of wintergreen ≈ 7 g of aspirin
pitfall: The concentration is what kills. A single teaspoon exceeds the lethal dose for a small child, and the exposure is often dismissed because the product is a topical rub or a flavouring. Salicylate levels must be followed serially; a single early level is falsely reassuring because absorption from the oil is prolonged.

dose:
Airway and aspiration precautions; no induced emesis
Pennyroyal: acetylcysteine as for acetaminophen hepatotoxicity
Wintergreen: treat as salicylate
pitfall: Two of these are not like the others. Wintergreen is salicylate and pennyroyal is hepatotoxic through a NAPQI-like metabolite; both need specific management while the rest need only aspiration precautions. The rise of concentrated oils sold for diffusers has made paediatric exposures more severe than the historical literature suggests.

dose:
Fluid resuscitation and electrolyte correction; haemodialysis in massive ingestion with renal failure
Activated charcoal does not bind boric acid
pitfall: The classic 'boiled lobster' erythroderma with desquamation follows a large ingestion, along with vomiting and blue-green emesis. Most household exposures are trivial; the dangerous ones are chronic or massive. Charcoal is useless here, which is easy to forget when reaching for a reflex decontamination.

dose:
Check G6PD status where possible; methylene blue only if G6PD-replete
Exchange transfusion for severe haemolysis
Supportive care; monitor haemoglobin and bilirubin for several days
pitfall: Naphthalene causes haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia, most severely in G6PD deficiency — the same population in whom methylene blue is contraindicated. Distinguish naphthalene from paradichlorobenzene mothballs, which are far less toxic: naphthalene balls sink in saturated salt water, paradichlorobenzene floats.

agentLine: None — this is a surgical emergency
dose:
Immediate radiograph; oesophageal lodgement requires endoscopic removal within 2 h
Honey 10 mL every 10 min (age >12 months, <12 h since ingestion) while awaiting removal
Nothing by mouth otherwise; do not induce vomiting
pitfall: Mucosal burn begins within 2 hours of oesophageal lodgement and perforation or aortoenteric fistula can follow days later. The child may be entirely asymptomatic. A coin and a battery look similar on film — the double-ring or halo sign identifies the battery, and getting this wrong costs the oesophagus.
window: Endoscopic removal within 2 h of oesophageal lodgement

dose:
Radiograph in two planes; multiple magnets or a magnet plus any metal object requires urgent removal
A single magnet with no other metallic foreign body may be observed
pitfall: Two magnets in different bowel loops attract across the walls and cause pressure necrosis, fistula, volvulus, and perforation — often days later and often without early symptoms. Counting the magnets on the film is the whole assessment; magnets stacked in a line can be mistaken for one.

dose:
Airway and antiemetics; benzodiazepines for seizures; atropine for bronchorrhoea and bradycardia
Skin decontamination for dermal exposure to concentrate
pitfall: Concentrated refill liquid is a paediatric lethal-dose problem: a few millilitres can kill a toddler. The picture is biphasic — early nicotinic stimulation with vomiting and tachycardia, then a depressive phase with bradycardia, weakness, and respiratory failure. The apparent improvement between phases is not recovery.

dose:
Remove from exposure; humidified oxygen; bronchodilators
Observe for delayed pulmonary oedema in significant exposures
pitfall: Almost always a domestic cleaning accident and almost always self-limiting, but a closed bathroom changes that. Nebulised bicarbonate is popular for chlorine and poorly supported; oxygen and bronchodilators are the treatment. Ask specifically what was mixed — the history is often given as 'cleaning fumes'.

dose:
Dextrose and monitoring for hypoglycaemia, particularly in children
Airway protection; check for co-ingested methanol in counterfeit product
pitfall: Small children develop hypoglycaemia and profound CNS depression at ethanol levels adults tolerate. Counterfeit and improperly manufactured sanitizer has been found to contain methanol, so an unexpectedly severe presentation with acidosis or visual symptoms should prompt a toxic alcohol workup rather than reassurance.

agentLine: None — bicarbonate, epinephrine, aggressive potassium caution
dose:
Early intubation and sedation; sodium bicarbonate for QRS widening
Epinephrine infusion for hypotension
Replace potassium cautiously — hypokalaemia is intracellular shift and rebounds
Diazepam has been used in high dose; evidence is historical
pitfall: One or two adult tablets can kill a toddler, and deterioration is abrupt — from alert to arrest within an hour. The hypokalaemia is a shift, not a deficit, and aggressive replacement causes fatal rebound hyperkalaemia as the drug clears. Dialysis and charcoal haemoperfusion do not work; the volume of distribution is enormous.
window: Deterioration within 1–2 h of ingestion

dose:
Naloxone as for opioid toxicity, often by infusion
Admit and observe at least 24 h regardless of an asymptomatic interval
pitfall: The trap is the delayed and biphasic course: an early anticholinergic phase from atropine, then opioid respiratory depression as diphenoxylate is metabolised, appearing up to 12 hours after ingestion. Any paediatric exposure is admitted. Discharging a well child at 6 hours has killed children.
window: Opioid effect may not appear for up to 12 h

dose:
Benzodiazepines for seizures; wash the skin thoroughly
No oil-based products on the skin — they increase absorption
pitfall: Seizures follow both ingestion and excessive topical use, and the highest-risk group is small, thin children treated for scabies with repeated applications. Oil-based emollients applied over lindane substantially increase systemic absorption.

dose:
Supportive care; monitor for delayed bone marrow suppression and neuropathy
Remove any remaining topical product
pitfall: A prolonged and biphasic illness: gastrointestinal upset and CNS depression early, then marrow suppression and a sensorimotor neuropathy over days to weeks. Systemic toxicity from topical application to large or mucosal surfaces is well described, especially in pregnancy where it is contraindicated.

dose:
Observation and supportive care; benzodiazepines for agitation
ECG for QT — citalopram and escitalopram prolong it dose-dependently
Watch for serotonin syndrome if a second serotonergic agent is involved
pitfall: Isolated SSRI overdose is usually benign, and the error is over-treating it. The exceptions are citalopram and escitalopram, where QT prolongation and seizures occur at high doses and warrant cardiac monitoring, and any co-ingestion that makes serotonin syndrome possible.

dose:
Sodium bicarbonate for QRS widening; benzodiazepines for seizures
Cardiac monitoring; extended-release preparations delay the peak
pitfall: Massive overdose produces sodium channel blockade indistinguishable from tricyclic toxicity, which is not what most clinicians expect from an antiepileptic. Separately, a rash in a patient on lamotrigine is a different emergency — Stevens-Johnson syndrome — and must not be dismissed.

dose:
MDAC 25 g q4h if bowel sounds present
EXTRIP: dialysis for severe toxicity, refractory seizures, or life-threatening dysrhythmia
Cardiac monitoring; anticholinergic features are common
pitfall: Absorption is erratic and prolonged, so levels rise for many hours and a plateau is not a peak. Carbamazepine is one of the few poisonings where multi-dose charcoal has real evidence behind it. Cyclic coma with fluctuating consciousness is characteristic and is often mistaken for improvement.

dose:
Stop the infusion; supportive care
EXTRIP suggests extracorporeal removal only in severe toxicity
Purple glove syndrome and hypotension are infusion-rate related
pitfall: Oral overdose causes ataxia, nystagmus, and coma but is rarely fatal. The dangerous route is intravenous: rapid infusion causes hypotension and asystole from the propylene glycol diluent, not the phenytoin. Fosphenytoin avoids this and should be used where rapid loading is needed.

dose:
Supportive care; benzodiazepines for agitation
ECG for QT; avoid additional QT-prolonging agents
Anticholinergic and alpha-blocking features are common
pitfall: Quetiapine produces deep sedation and tachycardia that reliably prompts intubation, and most patients would have woken on their own. Olanzapine can cause a fluctuating agitated delirium alternating with coma. Physostigmine is not appropriate here despite the antimuscarinic features, because of the sodium channel and QT effects.

dose:
Supportive care; benzodiazepines
Cyclobenzaprine is structurally a tricyclic — monitor QRS
Tizanidine causes marked hypotension and bradycardia
pitfall: Cyclobenzaprine's tricyclic structure means large overdoses produce sodium channel blockade and anticholinergic delirium, which surprises people who file it under 'muscle relaxant'. Tizanidine is an alpha-2 agonist and behaves like clonidine.

dose:
Sodium bicarbonate for QRS widening; magnesium for torsades
Multi-dose activated charcoal
Ophthalmology involvement for visual loss
pitfall: Blindness from retinal toxicity is the feature that separates quinine from other antiarrhythmics, and it can be permanent. Historical treatments aimed at increasing elimination — stellate ganglion block, aggressive dialysis — do not work and have been abandoned. Quinine in leg-cramp remedies remains a source of exposure.

dose:
Supportive care; atropine and pacing for bradycardia
Acute oral overdose is usually well tolerated
pitfall: Acute overdose is far less dangerous than the chronic drug. The real toxicities — pulmonary fibrosis, thyroid dysfunction, hepatitis, optic neuropathy — accumulate over months and present as a diagnostic problem, not a poisoning. Intravenous loading causes hypotension from the polysorbate diluent.

dose:
Supportive care and observation
Haemodialysis clears both, rarely required except in renal failure
pitfall: Overdose alone is usually benign; the danger is additive respiratory depression with opioids, and gabapentinoids now appear in a large share of opioid deaths. In renal impairment, therapeutic doses accumulate and produce myoclonus and encephalopathy that is regularly misread as a neurological event.

dose:
Sodium bicarbonate for QRS widening; magnesium for torsades
Naloxone does not reverse the cardiac toxicity
Prolonged cardiac monitoring — the half-life is long
pitfall: Taken in gram quantities for opioid effect or withdrawal self-treatment, loperamide blocks cardiac sodium and potassium channels and causes syncope, torsades, and sudden death. Naloxone addresses the opioid effect and does nothing for the dysrhythmia, which is what kills.

sources.label: FDA safety communication on loperamide abuse

dose:
Benzodiazepines for agitation; supportive care
Watch for serotonin syndrome with concurrent serotonergic agents
Check the preparation for acetaminophen
pitfall: Combination cough products are the hidden hazard: an adolescent taking a large dose for dissociative effect may also be taking a large dose of acetaminophen. Check the formulation and send a paracetamol level before attributing everything to dextromethorphan.

dose:
Benzodiazepines for emergence agitation; supportive care
Chronic use: ulcerative cystitis and biliary tract disease
pitfall: Acute recreational overdose is rarely lethal alone and is dangerous mainly through aspiration, trauma, and co-ingestion. Chronic heavy use causes a severe ulcerative cystitis with contracted bladder and obstructive uropathy that is frequently missed because the urinary complaint is not connected to the drug history.

dose:
Benzodiazepines generously for agitation, hypertension, and chest pain
Aspirin and nitroglycerin for ischaemia; phentolamine for refractory hypertension
Active cooling for hyperthermia; sodium bicarbonate for QRS widening
pitfall: Benzodiazepines treat almost everything here because the driver is central sympathetic outflow. Beta-blockade during the acute sympathomimetic surge risks unopposed alpha stimulation and is avoided. Hyperthermia and agitated delirium, not the cardiac effects, are what kill in the emergency department.

sources.label: AHA scientific statement on cocaine-associated chest pain

dose:
Benzodiazepines titrated to sedation; active cooling
IV fluids; monitor creatine kinase and renal function
Antipsychotics worsen hyperthermia and lower the seizure threshold
pitfall: Hyperthermia with agitated delirium is the lethal syndrome and it needs sedation and cooling within minutes, not physical restraint. Restraint alone increases isometric heat production and lactate. If sedation fails, intubate and paralyse.

dose:
Benzodiazepines; active cooling
Check sodium — hyponatraemia from SIADH plus free-water intake is common
Hypertonic saline for symptomatic hyponatraemia
pitfall: Two mechanisms compete and the treatment differs. Hyperthermia needs cooling and sedation; hyponatraemic seizures need hypertonic saline and fluid restriction. Giving free water to a hyperthermic MDMA patient with SIADH has caused fatal cerebral oedema, mostly in young women.

dose:
Benzodiazepines in large doses; active cooling; IV fluids
Monitor creatine kinase, potassium, and renal function
pitfall: Agitation is often far more severe and prolonged than with cocaine or amphetamine, and doses of benzodiazepine that would sedate other patients fail. Routine urine drug screens do not detect these compounds, so a negative screen means nothing.

dose:
Benzodiazepines; supportive care
Consider brodifacoum contamination if there is unexplained bleeding — check INR
pitfall: Presentation ranges from somnolence to seizures, acute kidney injury, and myocardial ischaemia in young people, none of which resembles cannabis. Contamination with long-acting anticoagulant rodenticide has caused outbreaks of severe coagulopathy; an unexplained raised INR in this population is the clue.

dose:
Avoid catecholamines where possible — the myocardium is sensitised
Toluene: expect severe hypokalaemia, non-anion-gap acidosis, and weakness
Supportive care and observation
pitfall: Sudden sniffing death is a catecholamine-sensitised ventricular dysrhythmia, so a startled or physically restrained user is at real risk and epinephrine is relatively contraindicated. Chronic toluene abuse produces a distal renal tubular acidosis with profound hypokalaemia presenting as quadriparesis.

dose:
Supportive care; naloxone for respiratory depression, response is variable
Benzodiazepines for seizures and agitation
Manage withdrawal as opioid withdrawal
pitfall: Sold as a herbal supplement and taken as one, so patients frequently do not report it as a drug. It has genuine opioid activity, causes dependence and a withdrawal syndrome, and has caused hepatotoxicity and seizures. Deaths are usually in combination with other sedatives.

agentLine: None — B12 replacement for neurological injury
dose:
Acute: oxygen and supportive care
Chronic: hydroxocobalamin or cyanocobalamin, methionine, folate
Check B12, homocysteine, and methylmalonic acid — B12 may be normal
pitfall: Heavy chronic use inactivates vitamin B12 and produces subacute combined degeneration of the cord: paraesthesia, ataxia, and myelopathy in a young person. The serum B12 can be entirely normal because the vitamin is present but functionally inactive — homocysteine and methylmalonic acid are the tests that show it.

dose:
Wash the skin; vitamin E oil for paraesthesia
Benzodiazepines for the rare seizure
Supportive care; most exposures are mild
pitfall: The commonest presentation is facial and hand paraesthesia after dermal contact, which resolves without treatment. Severe systemic toxicity is rare and usually reflects the hydrocarbon solvent rather than the pyrethroid. Anaphylaxis to pyrethrins occurs and is a separate problem.

dose:
Aggressive fluid resuscitation; correct acidosis; airway protection
Monitor for corrosive gastrointestinal injury and renal failure
Haemodialysis for severe acidosis or renal failure
pitfall: The surfactant, not the glyphosate, drives the toxicity — hypotension, corrosive injury, and pulmonary oedema after large deliberate ingestion. Small dermal or spray exposures are usually trivial, which makes the severe deliberate ingestions easy to underestimate.

dose: Wash the skin; supportive care; benzodiazepines for seizures
pitfall: Reported encephalopathy and seizures are almost entirely from ingestion or from heavy, repeated application to young children under occlusion. Normal repellent use is safe, and reassurance is usually the correct intervention.

dose:
Remove from the environment; 100% oxygen; supportive care
No antidote — the injury is hypoxic, not toxic
pitfall: Scene safety dominates. Confined-space deaths regularly claim the would-be rescuer, and multiple casualties at one scene should be assumed to be an oxygen-displaced atmosphere until proven otherwise. Carbon dioxide additionally causes narcosis and acidosis rather than pure displacement.

dose:
Exchange transfusion for massive haemolysis; haemodialysis for renal failure
Aggressive hydration and alkalinisation
Chelation is ineffective and should not delay transfusion
pitfall: This is not arsenic poisoning and must not be treated as such. Arsine causes explosive intravascular haemolysis with abdominal pain, dark urine, and jaundice within hours, followed by renal failure. Chelators do not bind arsine, and reaching for BAL wastes the window for exchange transfusion.

dose:
Remove from exposure; supportive care
Monitor for delayed pulmonary oedema and neurological injury
Protect responders — residual gas persists in treated structures
pitfall: Neurological injury and pulmonary oedema are delayed by hours to days, so an asymptomatic exposed worker cannot be cleared early. Structural fumigation incidents have poisoned families who re-entered a treated building prematurely.

agentLine: None — supportive; antivenom is not available in the US
dose:
Remove stingers; aggressive fluid resuscitation
Monitor creatine kinase, potassium, renal function, and haemolysis for several days
Epinephrine and standard anaphylaxis care if that component is present
pitfall: Two entirely different illnesses share the presentation. Anaphylaxis from a single sting kills within minutes; envenomation syndrome from hundreds of stings kills over days through rhabdomyolysis, haemolysis, and renal failure. Africanized bees are established across South Texas and mass attacks occur.

dose:
Local wound care; do not unroof the sterile pustules
Antihistamines and analgesia; epinephrine for anaphylaxis
pitfall: The sterile pustule at 24 hours is characteristic and is not infection — treating it with antibiotics or unroofing it invites secondary infection. Anaphylaxis is the real risk and warrants an adrenaline autoinjector prescription in anyone with a systemic reaction.

dose:
Detach the animal; irrigate and radiograph for retained teeth
Analgesia and fluid resuscitation for hypotension
Observe for angio-oedema
pitfall: The animal holds on and chews, so retained teeth in the wound are common and are the usual source of persistent problems. Hypotension can be marked and out of proportion to the local wound. No antivenom exists anywhere.

dose:
Supportive care and analgesia; amitriptyline or gabapentin for chronic dysaesthesia
Intravenous mannitol has been used and is not supported by controlled evidence
Advise avoidance of fish, alcohol, nuts, and caffeine during recovery
pitfall: The signature is reversal of hot and cold sensation with paraesthesia after eating a large reef fish, and it can persist for months. Cooking does not destroy the toxin. Recurrence is provoked by alcohol and by eating fish again, so dietary advice at discharge is part of the treatment.

dose:
H1 and H2 antihistamines; this is a histamine reaction, not an allergy
Epinephrine rarely needed; supportive care
pitfall: Flushing, headache, and palpitations shortly after eating a peppery-tasting tuna, mahi-mahi, or mackerel. It is regularly misdiagnosed as fish allergy, and the consequence is a patient told to avoid fish for life for a condition caused by spoilage. Other diners becoming ill supports the diagnosis.

dose:
Airway protection and mechanical ventilation until the block resolves
Supportive care; there is no antidote
pitfall: Ascending paralysis with a completely preserved sensorium, so the patient is aware and terrified throughout — sedate them. Survival is a function of ventilation alone. Recovery is usually complete within 24 hours if the airway was secured in time.

dose:
Airway protection and ventilation; supportive care
No antidote; symptoms typically resolve within 24 h
pitfall: Perioral paraesthesia within an hour of eating bivalves during a red tide, progressing to weakness and respiratory paralysis. Cooking does not destroy saxitoxin and the shellfish are not visibly abnormal. Ask about others who ate the same meal.

agentLine: None. Decontamination in the first minutes is the only thing that changes this patient; after that it is burn, ocular and airway care
dose:
No antidote and no FDA-approved countermeasure exists
Decontaminate: remove all clothing → blot liquid agent off without spreading it → copious soap and water. Reduces tissue damage only within 1–2 min of exposure
Eyes: copious irrigation with water or 0.9% sodium chloride → topical antibiotic, mydriatic for ciliary spasm
Airway: humidified oxygen; nebulised bronchodilator; bronchoscopy to clear the pseudomembrane
Skin: manage as partial and full-thickness burn — do not use burn fluid formulas for mustard blisters
Daily CBC. Leukocytes fall from day 3–5 with nadir near day 9; a count of 500 or fewer predicts a poor outcome
pitfall: The latent period is what kills. A vapour-exposed patient can look completely well for 2 to 48 hours, gets triaged as exposed-but-fine, and goes home undecontaminated — returning with deep burns and an obstructing airway cast. Decontamination after the lesions appear is too late to help that patient but is still not optional, because mustard on skin and clothing transfers to staff and turns the department into the second incident site. The third failure is discharging a burn patient with no haematological plan: leukocytes fall from day 3 to 5 with a nadir near day 9, and the deaths at days 3 to 6 are secondary bacterial pneumonia in a marrow-suppressed host, not the blisters. Airway casts get treated as asthma when they need bronchoscopic removal.
window: Decontamination prevents injury only within 1–2 min (ATSDR; JTS gives 3–5 min). Signs appear 2 h after heavy liquid exposure and as late as 48 h after low-dose vapour

agentLine: Dimercaprol (BAL in Oil) deep IM — for systemic arsenical toxicity only. It does nothing for the skin lesion
dose:
FDA label, severe arsenic poisoning: 3 mg/kg deep IM q4h × 2 days → 4 times on day 3 → twice daily for 10 days
FDA label, mild arsenic poisoning: 2.5 mg/kg deep IM 4 times daily × 2 days → twice on day 3 → once daily for 10 days
Lewisite, guideline (off-label for this agent): 3–5 mg/kg deep IM q4h × 4 doses (ATSDR); or 3 mg/kg q4h × 2 days → q12h for 7–10 days (JTS)
Deep intramuscular only — never IV. Supplied 100 mg/mL; each 1 mL carries 200 mg benzyl benzoate and 700 mg peanut oil
Alkalinise the urine throughout — the dimercaprol–arsenic complex dissociates in acid urine. Stop for acute renal insufficiency
No topical BAL skin or ophthalmic ointment is marketed in the US
Decontaminate at once with copious water; lewisite penetrates skin in seconds
pitfall: Immediate searing pain is the triage discriminator — mustard is painless for hours, lewisite and phosgene oxime hurt instantly — so a screaming casualty does not exclude a vesicant and a comfortable one does not exclude mustard, and reversing that inverts your decontamination urgency for the whole incident. BAL treats the systemic arsenical and has no effect on the local lesion, so giving it to a patient you have not decontaminated treats nothing. The drug is the second trap: deep IM only, in a peanut-oil and benzyl-benzoate vehicle, so an IV push and a peanut-allergic patient are two ways the antidote kills; and because the complex breaks down in acid urine, failing to alkalinise turns the chelator into a nephrotoxin. Confirm stock before you need it — the Akorn product was discontinued in 2023, the application is now active under Provepharm, and no marketed NDC is listed.
window: Immediate pain on contact — there is no latent period to work inside. BAL is not prophylactic: start it when systemic toxicity appears (lewisite shock, hypotension, significant pulmonary injury)

agentLine: None specific. Enforced rest, humidified oxygen, lung-protective ventilation with PEEP if ARDS develops — and do not diurese
dose:
No antidote exists
Enforced rest from the moment of exposure — carry the patient, do not let them walk. On discharge: no vigorous activity for 1–2 days
Humidified oxygen for dyspnoea or hypoxaemia; nebulised bronchodilator for bronchospasm; racemic epinephrine for stridor
Observe every exposed patient. Asymptomatic with a normal examination and no signs of toxicity after 48 h of observation may be discharged (ATSDR)
Corticosteroids: suggested by ATSDR for intense epithelial inflammation, but no controlled human evidence exists
Diuretics are contraindicated — this is permeability oedema with intravascular depletion
Nebulised N-acetylcysteine failed in a controlled porcine model; do not substitute it for observation
pitfall: Phosgene is dangerous precisely because the patient feels well and therefore moves: even minimal exertion during the latent period shortens it and worsens the lung injury, so walking a comfortable patient through decontamination, down to radiology or out to the car is itself a therapeutic error — ATSDR states that any activity after exposure may increase the likelihood of death. The second killer is the early discharge; onset is documented out to 72 hours and the rule is 48 hours of observation. Low-concentration exposure produces little upper-airway irritation, which is exactly why it reaches the alveoli — absence of eye and throat burning is reassuring in chlorine and is a red flag here. Do not reach for a drug: nebulised acetylcysteine failed in a controlled animal model, the steroid data are uncontrolled, and diuretics are contraindicated.
window: Asymptomatic latent period of 30 min to 72 h; severity shortens it. Dyspnoea within 4–6 h marks severe exposure. A normal chest film at 8 h makes pulmonary oedema unlikely, but the discharge threshold is still 48 h of observation

agentLine: None. Decontaminate in seconds, then wound, ocular and airway care with aggressive analgesia
dose:
No antidote exists
Decontamination is the only measure that reduces tissue damage and the window is seconds — CX is absorbed almost immediately. Remove clothing → copious water irrigation of skin and eyes
Parenteral opioid analgesia — immediate severe pain is the presenting problem
Wound care as for chemical necrosis; expect necrosis rather than blisters
Humidified oxygen and nebulised bronchodilator for airway involvement; watch for noncardiogenic pulmonary oedema
pitfall: CX is a corrosive urticant, not a true vesicant: immediate pain, a blanched area inside an erythematous ring, then frank necrosis and never a classic blister — so a responder looking for bullae concludes this is not a vesicant and stands decontamination down on a patient being destroyed faster than by mustard or lewisite. It penetrates clothing and rubber faster than the other agents and is absorbed within seconds, so nothing done at the door prevents the injury; decontaminate anyway, because what is on that patient is still corrosive to you. CX is weaponised in mixtures specifically to drive other agents through skin, so immediate pain without blisters should start a search for a co-agent rather than end in a diagnosis of irritant exposure.
window: Effects are immediate — there is no latent period. By the time the patient reaches the department the window has closed, and decontamination is then for staff protection and to stop spread

agentLine: Hydroxocobalamin empirically, 100% oxygen from first contact, and an early airway decision — carbon monoxide, cyanide and thermal injury arrive together and interact
dose:
HYDROXOCOBALAMIN (Cyanokit) — empiric, do not wait for a cyanide level
Adult 5 g IV over 15 min → a second 5 g over 15 min to 2 h for persistent coma, hypotension or acidosis, max total 10 g
Paediatric 70 mg/kg IV, not to exceed 5 g per dose (EMA posology; the US label states paediatric safety is not established)
Reconstitute each 5 g vial with 200 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride
SODIUM THIOSULFATE — optional adjunct after hydroxocobalamin; safe here but too slow alone. Adult 12.5 g IV; paediatric 250 mg/kg IV, not to exceed 12.5 g
SODIUM NITRITE — withhold unless hydroxocobalamin is unavailable and cyanide toxicity is life-threatening. It is cautioned, not contraindicated. If forced: adult 300 mg IV at 2.5–5 mL/min → thiosulfate immediately after; reduce the dose in proportion to the oxygen-carrying capacity already lost to carboxyhaemoglobin and keep methaemoglobin under 30%
OXYGEN 100% by non-rebreather or tube from first contact, continued until symptom-free
Hyperbaric referral: carboxyhaemoglobin above 25–30%, any loss of consciousness, neurological or cardiac involvement, severe acidosis — and any pregnant patient regardless of level
AIRWAY: intubate early for full-thickness facial burns, stridor, hoarseness, respiratory distress, oropharyngeal swelling on laryngoscopy, altered mentation, hypoxia or hypercarbia
pitfall: Draw the carboxyhaemoglobin, the lactate and the co-oximetry before the hydroxocobalamin runs, not after. Its deep red pigment falsifies laboratory co-oximetry and much of the chemistry panel — haemoglobin reads artificially high for 12 to 16 hours, coagulation studies are unpredictable for 24 to 48 — so the carboxyhaemoglobin you need to justify a hyperbaric transfer and the methaemoglobin you need to judge nitrite safety both become uninterpretable at the moment you need them, and the dialysis machine will later stop on a false blood-leak alarm. The second way this patient dies with everything else right is the airway: he is awake, talking and soot-stained, so he stays on a non-rebreather while laryngeal oedema builds, and the tube that was easy at hour one is a surgical airway at hour four. Pulse oximetry reads normal in carbon monoxide poisoning; singed nasal hair has a diagnostic odds ratio of 0.93, which is to say none — their absence is not clearance.
window: Give hydroxocobalamin within minutes of coma, seizure, arrest, systolic pressure under 90 mmHg, or a high lactate — lactate of 10 mmol/L or more in a fire victim without severe burns is the validated marker of blood cyanide above 40 µmol/L, and 8 mmol/L is the conservative operational trigger. Carboxyhaemoglobin half-life falls from about 4–5 h on room air to about 74 min on 100% oxygen

agentLine: Epinephrine, intramuscular, anterolateral thigh — the only drug that changes the outcome
dose:
Adult: epinephrine 1 mg/mL, 0.3–0.5 mg IM into the anterolateral thigh → repeat every 5–10 min as needed
Child under 30 kg: 0.01 mg/kg IM anterolateral thigh, up to 0.3 mg per dose → repeat every 5–10 min
Autoinjector: 0.3 mg at 30 kg or more; 0.15 mg at 15–30 kg; 0.1 mg at 7.5–15 kg. More than 2 sequential doses only under direct supervision
Nasal spray (neffy): 2 mg at 30 kg or more; 1 mg at 15 kg to under 30 kg → a second spray into the same nostril at 5 min if no improvement
Still anaphylactic after 2 IM doses: epinephrine infusion 1 mg in 1000 mL sodium chloride at 5 mL/kg/h, about 0.1 µg/kg/min, titrated → crystalloid 20 mL/kg, repeated up to 50 mL/kg in the first 30 min
On a beta-blocker and refractory: glucagon 1–2 mg IV in adults, 20–30 µg/kg up to 1 mg in children → 1–2 mg/h
Adjuncts only after epinephrine: H1 antihistamine for urticaria, nebulised albuterol for bronchospasm, oxygen, supine with legs raised
Corticosteroids are not indicated to prevent biphasic anaphylaxis
At discharge: autoinjector prescribed, baseline serum tryptase drawn, allergy referral for venom immunotherapy
pitfall: The patient who dies in a fully stocked resuscitation bay is the one who got diphenhydramine and methylprednisolone first and epinephrine at minute twelve — the steroid was never going to work acutely, and it does not prevent the biphasic reaction it is reflexively given for. The second failure is site and route: subcutaneous injection peaks at a mean of 34 minutes against 8 for intramuscular thigh, and the deltoid is inferior to the thigh, so a numerically correct dose in the arm is a late dose. The third is stopping at two autoinjectors — refractory anaphylaxis needs a titrated infusion and aggressive crystalloid, not a third handheld device, and a beta-blocked patient may not respond at all until glucagon bypasses the blocked receptor. Untreated systemic reactors face roughly a 50% risk on the next sting and immunotherapy drops it below 5%, so the referral belongs on the discharge paperwork, not on a wish list.
window: Give on suspicion, before diagnostic criteria are met. Median time to arrest in fatal venom anaphylaxis is 15 min. Observation is risk-stratified: a non-severe reaction that resolved on one dose and stays symptom-free for 1 h has a 95% negative predictive value for a biphasic reaction; severe reactions or more than one dose warrant observation toward 6 h

agentLine: No antidote and none is needed. The tick is the treatment — find it and take it off
dose:
Find and remove the tick. That is the entire treatment; no antitoxin is obtainable in the United States
Undress the patient completely → search scalp and hairline, behind and inside the ears, nape, axillae, groin, perineum, umbilicus, interdigital webs → part and comb long or matted hair in sections under good light
Grasp with fine forceps as close to the skin as possible → steady upward traction, no twisting, no squeezing the body → remove mouthparts and salivary glands intact, because the salivary gland is the toxin source
No improvement at 48 h → search again for a second tick, then question the diagnosis
Supportive only: serial vital capacity and negative inspiratory force, airway protection and ventilation until the toxin clears
No role for IVIG, plasma exchange, corticosteroids, anticholinesterase or antivenom
pitfall: The killer is the tick nobody finds. A child is intubated for presumed Guillain-Barré, given IVIG, then plasma exchange, and keeps deteriorating for days because an engorged Dermacentor sits under matted hair behind an ear and nobody undressed and combed the patient — misdiagnosis as Guillain-Barré has become more frequent over recent decades, not less. The discriminators are free at the bedside: the cerebrospinal fluid is normal with no albuminocytologic dissociation, the sensory examination is normal despite paraesthesias, and although ptosis and dilated pupils overlap with botulism, botulism descends from the cranial nerves while this ascends from the legs. Do not anchor on the classic young girl with long hair — modern series are full of adults of both sexes, and that picture is a historical skew rather than a rule.
window: Toxin delivery peaks on days 5–7 of attachment, so the tick is engorged and findable by the time weakness appears. After removal of a Dermacentor tick improvement begins within hours and recovery is complete in about 24–48 h. Australian Ixodes holocyclus cases characteristically worsen for 24–48 h after removal and are observed, not discharged

agentLine: No specific antidote. Aggressive shock management, early VA-ECMO conversation, and staff protection from off-gassing
dose:
Decontamination: NG lavage with sodium bicarbonate or 1:10,000 potassium permanganate → activated charcoal 1 g/kg NG
Coconut oil 100–200 mL PO/NG — contested; mortality signal in meta-analysis, no RCT
Magnesium sulfate 3 g IV bolus → 6 g over 24 h infusion — contested
N-acetylcysteine 150 mg/kg over 1 h → 50 mg/kg over 4 h → 100 mg/kg over 16 h — weak evidence
Norepinephrine and vasopressin titrated to MAP ≥65 mmHg; sodium bicarbonate for pH <7.1
Call VA-ECMO on suspicion of significant ingestion — cannulation before the second arrest correlates with survival
pitfall: Staff and family inhale phosphine off the patient's vomitus and NG aspirate — SCBA in the resuscitation bay, vent aspirate outside, or the code team gets exposed. Coconut oil and magnesium are reflex interventions in South Asian EDs and no controlled trial has shifted mortality; the time they steal is time that would help more if spent on high-dose vasopressors and a VA-ECMO conversation before the first arrest.
window: Cardiogenic shock peaks 12–24 h; hepatorenal injury 72–96 h. Early ECMO — before, not after, the arrest

agentLine: No specific antidote. 100% oxygen, serial COHb, and observation long enough to catch the delayed CO peak
dose:
Remove from source; 100% non-rebreather, intubate if obtunded
Serial COHb every 2 h for 12–24 h — the first level is often falsely reassuring
Hyperbaric oxygen only when standard CO triggers apply (LOC, ischaemia, seizure, pregnancy, COHb >25%); ATSDR notes MC-derived CO is usually not itself an HBO indication because endogenous conversion continues after the dive
Supportive: fluids, benzodiazepine for agitation or seizure, monitor LFTs (hepatotoxicity 24–72 h)
Discharge threshold: asymptomatic 6–12 h post-exposure for mild exposures only (ATSDR)
pitfall: The refinisher walks in with a headache and normal SpO₂, an early COHb of 8%, and gets sent home — then seizes at hour 10 because CYP2E1 kept metabolising stored DCM into CO all afternoon. Pulse oximetry is blind to dyshaemoglobinaemia. Trend the COHb; do not rely on the first one, and do not rush to the hyperbaric chamber unless the trigger would apply to any CO poisoning — the metabolism outlasts the dive.
window: CYP2E1 keeps turning stored DCM into carbon monoxide for hours after the exposure ends — COHb continues to rise for hours and stays elevated 1–2 days. Do not discharge on a single low level

agentLine: No antidote. If a peri-arrest arrhythmia is present, reach for a beta-blocker first, not epinephrine
dose:
Remove from source, 100% oxygen, cardiac monitor
Sudden sniffing death — VF/VT precipitated by catecholamine surge: esmolol 500 µg/kg IV load → 50–200 µg/kg/min, OR propranolol 1 mg IV, repeat every 2 min up to 5 mg — AVOID epinephrine as first-line pressor
Amiodarone 300 mg IV or lidocaine 1–1.5 mg/kg if beta-blockade contraindicated
Correct potassium aggressively — chronic deficits often 200–400 mEq; monitor phosphate and magnesium for rhabdomyolysis
Sodium bicarbonate only for severe acidaemia (pH <7.1); does not reverse the underlying renal tubular acidosis
pitfall: Two failure modes kill. First — the young huffer arrests during restraint, gets epinephrine 1 mg reflexively, and stays in refractory VF because the sensitised myocardium needed a beta-blocker and the ACLS drug was wrong. Second — the weak young patient with potassium 1.9, non-anion-gap acidosis and paint on the face is treated as periodic paralysis or laxative abuse and discharged after potassium replacement, returning intubated with rhabdomyolysis. Miss the chronic distal RTA and you miss the diagnosis.
window: Sudden sniffing death occurs within minutes of the catecholamine trigger (police chase, startle, exertion). Sensitisation persists hours after the last huff

agentLine: Historical antidote dithiocarb is not on any US shelf. Admit every confirmed exposure regardless of early symptoms, and manage the delayed ARDS
dose:
Admit ANY confirmed exposure for at least 48 h regardless of the initial examination
100% oxygen; lung-protective ventilation if ARDS develops
Sodium diethyldithiocarbamate (dithiocarb, DDC) — historical Sunderman protocol 25 mg/kg PO ×1 → 12.5 mg/kg PO q4h × 4 days; parenteral 12.5 mg/kg IV or IM for severe cases. NOT FDA-approved, no US commercial supply, contested efficacy, animal data suggest DDC increases brain nickel uptake
Disulfiram 500 mg PO as an in-vivo DDC precursor has been proposed — off-label, weak evidence
Contact regional Poison Center 1-800-222-1222 on suspicion
pitfall: The refinery worker feels better by hour 4, is discharged from occupational health, and dies at hour 20 from an ARDS he never developed while anyone was watching — any confirmed exposure is admitted, full stop. Dithiocarb is not on any US pharmacy shelf; do not promise it to the family, do not delay ventilator support waiting for a compounding pharmacy, and do not accept a compounding lag as a reason to hold lung-protective ventilation.
window: The chest film is typically normal at presentation. Pulmonary oedema peaks 12–36 h after exposure. Urinary nickel above 100 µg/L in the first 8 h predicts a severe course

agentLine: Hydroxocobalamin on suspicion. Vent the room and don SCBA — HCN off-gasses from vomitus and NG aspirate and can poison the code team
dose:
Hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit) 5 g IV over 15 min → repeat 5 g if persistent instability, max 10 g total
Paediatric 70 mg/kg IV, not to exceed 5 g per dose (EMA posology; US label states paediatric safety not established)
Sodium thiosulfate 12.5 g IV push adult (50 mL of 25%); paediatric 400 mg/kg IV, not to exceed 12.5 g — additive to hydroxocobalamin
Activated charcoal 1 g/kg NG only if airway protected and within 1 h — cyanide is poorly adsorbed but the pill mass is small
Gastric lavage generally not attempted in the symptomatic patient — HCN off-gassing endangers staff; if attempted, N95 or SCBA and vent aspirate outside
Avoid amyl and sodium nitrite in the pure oral ingestion — hydroxocobalamin is preferred and methaemoglobinaemia adds risk without CO co-exposure to balance
pitfall: Vomitus and gastric aspirate from an oral cyanide patient in an unventilated resuscitation bay have poisoned code teams — this has killed responders. Vent the room, don SCBA, and do not bend over an unintubated airway. A single 5 g hydroxocobalamin dose is often inadequate for gram-scale KCN or NaCN — give the second 5 g early rather than waiting to see whether the first one worked, because by the time it is clear it did not, the patient has arrested.
window: Symptomatic within minutes. Give hydroxocobalamin on suspicion, before whole-blood cyanide returns and before the second cardiac arrest

agentLine: No antidote. Remove from source, benzodiazepine for agitation, standard ACLS for arrhythmia — and file the occupational report
dose:
Remove from source; decontaminate skin (dermal absorption is significant) and eyes
100% oxygen and airway support
Lorazepam 2–4 mg IV, repeat, for agitation or seizure
Standard ACLS for arrhythmia — no antidote
Report the exposure to OSHA and refer for industrial-hygiene air sampling; no ED chelation or dialysis intervention
OSHA PEL 20 ppm 8-h TWA (ceiling 30 ppm, 100 ppm 30-min peak, skin notation); NIOSH REL 1 ppm; IDLH 500 ppm
pitfall: A rayon or cellophane worker in his 40s with new chest pain and a clean troponin is admitted as acute coronary syndrome, discharged when the workup is negative, and returns in six months with an MI — the real problem was CS₂-driven coronary vasospasm on top of accelerated atherosclerosis, and the plant air was out of PEL. No ED drug fixes that. Document the exposure in the chart, file the occupational report, and get an industrial-hygiene walk-through, or you will treat the sequela of the exposure without touching the exposure.
window: Acute intoxication resolves with removal and supportive care. Chronic parkinsonism, neuropathy and accelerated coronary disease accrue over years — the ED visit matters mainly as the trigger for occupational surveillance
